notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Learning is a relatively lasting change in knowledge, skill or understanding resulting from experience or practice.
  • Learning involves acquiring, processing, storing and using information.
  • Memorisation and understanding are different components of learning.
  • Rote learning mainly depends on repetition and recall.
  • Conceptual learning focuses on understanding ideas, relationships and underlying principles.
  • Rote learning can help remember basic facts, formulas, definitions and sequences.
  • Conceptual learning helps apply knowledge to unfamiliar situations.
  • Effective learning generally combines necessary factual memory with conceptual understanding.
  • Memorising information without understanding it may produce correct recall but weak application.
  • Understanding a concept makes it easier to connect new information with existing knowledge.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rote Learning → Memorisation

Conceptual Learning → Understanding + Application

2. Rote Learning
  • Rote learning is learning through repetition without necessarily understanding the underlying meaning.
  • It is commonly used to memorise facts, definitions, formulas, dates and lists.
  • Repeated recitation is a common rote-learning technique.
  • Rote learning can produce rapid recall of familiar information.
  • It is useful when exact information must be remembered.
  • Multiplication tables can initially be learned through repetition.
  • Chemical symbols may require direct memorisation.
  • Scientific constants often require memorisation.
  • Vocabulary and terminology may also require rote recall.
  • Rote learning alone is less effective for solving unfamiliar problems.
  • Information learned only by rote may be forgotten if it is not revised regularly.
  • Rote learning does not automatically guarantee understanding.
📌 Remember

Rote Learning → Repeat → Memorise → Recall

3. Conceptual Learning
  • Conceptual learning involves understanding the meaning and relationships behind information.
  • It focuses on why and how rather than only what.
  • Conceptual learning helps learners connect new ideas with previously learned concepts.
  • It enables the application of knowledge to new situations.
  • Conceptual learning supports problem-solving.
  • It improves the ability to explain a phenomenon in one's own words.
  • Conceptual understanding helps identify similarities and differences between related ideas.
  • It supports long-term retention when concepts are meaningfully connected.
  • Conceptual learning is important in science because scientific topics are interconnected.
  • Understanding a principle is generally more useful than memorising an isolated example of the principle.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Conceptual Learning → Understand → Connect → Apply → Solve

4. Rote Learning vs Conceptual Learning
  • Rote learning emphasises repetition.
  • Conceptual learning emphasises understanding.
  • Rote learning is useful for recalling exact facts.
  • Conceptual learning is useful for applying principles.
  • Rote learning may depend heavily on repeated rehearsal.
  • Conceptual learning depends on relationships and meaning.
  • Rote knowledge may remain isolated.
  • Conceptual knowledge is integrated with other knowledge.
  • Rote learning may be sufficient for direct-recall questions.
  • Conceptual learning is particularly important for analytical and application-based questions.
  • Rote and conceptual learning are not always mutually exclusive.
  • Facts remembered through rote learning can serve as building blocks for conceptual understanding.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rote learning is not completely useless.

Conceptual learning does not eliminate the need to memorise essential facts.

5. Memorisation
  • Memorisation is the process of committing information to memory.
  • Memorisation may involve repetition, association or organisation.
  • Repetition strengthens familiarity with information.
  • Meaningful information is generally easier to remember than unrelated information.
  • Organising information into categories can improve recall.
  • Connecting new information with existing knowledge improves retention.
  • Memorisation is especially useful for information that cannot be logically derived each time.
  • Scientific symbols, units and certain constants require accurate memorisation.
6. Understanding
  • Understanding means grasping the meaning of information.
  • A learner who understands a concept can usually explain it using different words.
  • Understanding helps predict what may happen under changed conditions.
  • Understanding enables comparison between related concepts.
  • Understanding supports transfer of knowledge.
  • Correct answers do not always prove conceptual understanding if they were obtained only through memorisation.
  • Explanation and application are stronger indicators of understanding than simple repetition.
7. Recall
  • Recall is the retrieval of previously learned information from memory.
  • Free recall requires remembering information without being shown the answer.
  • Cued recall provides hints that assist retrieval.
  • Recognition involves identifying previously encountered information.
  • Multiple-choice questions often involve recognition as well as reasoning.
  • Recall generally requires more retrieval effort than recognition.
  • Frequent retrieval strengthens access to learned information.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Recall → Produce information

Recognition → Identify information

8. Recognition
  • Recognition is the ability to identify information that has been encountered before.
  • Recognition is generally easier than unaided recall.
  • Recognising the correct option in an MCQ does not always mean the concept can be explained independently.
  • Recognition can sometimes produce an illusion of mastery.
  • Active recall is useful for checking whether information can actually be retrieved without prompts.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Seeing an answer and thinking “I know this” is not the same as recalling it without help.

9. Memory
  • Memory enables information to be encoded, stored and retrieved.
  • Encoding is the process of converting information into a form that can be stored.
  • Storage refers to retaining information over time.
  • Retrieval is the process of accessing stored information.
  • Failure at any of these stages can result in poor recall.
  • Meaningful encoding generally improves later retrieval.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Encoding → Storage → Retrieval

10. Sensory Memory
  • Sensory memory briefly retains information received through the senses.
  • Visual sensory memory is called iconic memory.
  • Auditory sensory memory is called echoic memory.
  • Sensory memory lasts for a very short duration.
  • Attention determines which sensory information receives further processing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Visual sensory memory → Iconic

Auditory sensory memory → Echoic

11. Short-Term Memory
  • Short-term memory temporarily holds a limited amount of information.
  • Information in short-term memory can be lost quickly without rehearsal.
  • Repetition can help maintain information for a short period.
  • Short-term memory is closely related to the concept of working memory.
  • Working memory actively processes information while performing a task.
12. Working Memory
  • Working memory temporarily holds and manipulates information.
  • Mental calculation uses working memory.
  • Following multiple steps in a problem uses working memory.
  • Working memory has limited capacity.
  • Excessive information presented at once can overload working memory.
  • Organising information into meaningful groups can reduce the burden on working memory.
  • Prior knowledge can reduce working-memory demands by allowing information to be processed in larger meaningful units.
13. Long-Term Memory
  • Long-term memory stores information for extended periods.
  • Long-term memory includes knowledge, experiences and learned skills.
  • Repeated retrieval can strengthen long-term retention.
  • Meaningful associations help transfer information into long-term memory.
  • Conceptual understanding creates multiple connections that may aid retrieval.
  • Long-term memory is not a perfect permanent recording; memories can change or be forgotten.
14. Rehearsal
  • Rehearsal means repeating information to maintain or remember it.
  • Maintenance rehearsal involves simple repetition.
  • Elaborative rehearsal connects new information with meaning and existing knowledge.
  • Maintenance rehearsal is closely associated with rote memorisation.
  • Elaborative rehearsal supports deeper understanding and longer retention.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maintenance Rehearsal → Repeat

Elaborative Rehearsal → Connect with meaning

15. Meaningful Learning
  • Meaningful learning occurs when new knowledge is related to what the learner already knows.
  • Meaningful learning promotes understanding rather than isolated memorisation.
  • Prior knowledge plays an important role in meaningful learning.
  • Examples and analogies can help connect new concepts with familiar ideas.
  • Meaningful learning generally improves application and transfer.
  • David Ausubel is strongly associated with the theory of meaningful verbal learning.
  • Ausubel emphasised the importance of existing knowledge in learning new material.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

David Ausubel → Meaningful Learning → Prior Knowledge

16. Prior Knowledge
  • Prior knowledge is the information and understanding already possessed by a learner.
  • New learning is interpreted in relation to prior knowledge.
  • Correct prior knowledge can accelerate learning.
  • Incorrect prior knowledge can create misconceptions.
  • Activating relevant prior knowledge helps connect new concepts with familiar ideas.
  • Concept maps can reveal connections between existing and new knowledge.
17. Misconception
  • A misconception is an incorrect understanding of a concept.
  • Misconceptions can persist even after correct facts are memorised.
  • Conceptual learning requires identifying and correcting misconceptions.
  • Simply telling a learner the correct answer may not remove a deeply held misconception.
  • Contrasting incorrect and correct explanations can help conceptual change.
  • Experiments and demonstrations can challenge misconceptions by providing direct evidence.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Misconception → Wrong mental model, not merely forgotten information

18. Concept Formation
  • Concept formation involves grouping objects, events or ideas according to common characteristics.
  • A concept represents a general idea rather than one individual example.
  • Examples help learners identify defining characteristics of a concept.
  • Non-examples help distinguish a concept from similar concepts.
  • Classification is an important part of concept formation.
  • Scientific learning depends heavily on concept formation.
Example

Mammal → Concept

Cow → Example

Lizard → Non-example

19. Classification
  • Classification is the arrangement of objects or ideas into groups based on shared characteristics.
  • Classification reduces complexity and supports understanding.
  • Biological taxonomy is an example of scientific classification.
  • Elements are classified in the periodic table according to their properties and atomic structure.
  • Classification supports comparison and pattern recognition.
  • Effective classification depends on relevant criteria.
20. Generalisation
  • Generalisation involves applying a concept or rule beyond the original example.
  • Conceptual understanding allows appropriate generalisation.
  • Incorrect generalisation can occur when superficial similarities are mistaken for essential similarities.
  • Multiple examples help learners understand the range of a concept.
  • Non-examples help define the limits of a generalisation.
21. Transfer of Learning
  • Transfer of learning is the application of previously learned knowledge or skills to a new situation.
  • Positive transfer occurs when previous learning helps new learning.
  • Negative transfer occurs when previous learning interferes with new learning.
  • Near transfer occurs between similar situations.
  • Far transfer occurs when knowledge is applied to a substantially different situation.
  • Conceptual understanding improves the possibility of transfer.
  • Rote memorisation alone often produces weak transfer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Positive Transfer → Helps

Negative Transfer → Interferes

22. Positive Transfer
  • Positive transfer occurs when earlier learning improves performance in a new task.
  • Understanding basic arithmetic helps in learning algebra.
  • Knowledge of basic physics can assist in understanding mechanics.
  • Similar concepts and procedures can promote positive transfer.
  • Recognising underlying principles improves transfer.
23. Negative Transfer
  • Negative transfer occurs when previously learned knowledge or habits interfere with new learning.
  • Negative transfer can occur when two situations appear similar but follow different rules.
  • Prior misconceptions can cause negative transfer.
  • Identifying differences between old and new situations helps reduce negative transfer.
24. Learning by Association
  • Association links one piece of information with another.
  • Associations can improve recall.
  • Mnemonics use associations to support memory.
  • Associating scientific units with their physical quantities can aid memorisation.
  • Association can support both rote and meaningful learning depending on how it is used.
25. Mnemonics
  • A mnemonic is a memory aid.
  • Acronyms can be used as mnemonics.
  • Acrostics can help remember ordered information.
  • Rhymes and visual associations can also function as mnemonics.
  • Mnemonics assist recall but do not replace conceptual understanding.
  • A learner should understand the meaning of the items represented by a mnemonic.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mnemonic → Memory aid.

Mnemonic ≠ Conceptual explanation.

26. Chunking
  • Chunking means grouping individual pieces of information into larger meaningful units.
  • Chunking reduces the number of separate items that must be held in working memory.
  • Familiar patterns are easier to chunk than unrelated information.
  • Classification and grouping can improve memory through chunking.
  • Expertise allows complex information to be organised into meaningful chunks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chunking → Group information → Reduce working-memory load

27. Active Recall
  • Active recall means deliberately retrieving information from memory without looking at the answer.
  • Self-testing is a form of active recall.
  • Flashcards can support active recall when the answer is attempted before checking.
  • Practice questions support retrieval.
  • Active recall reveals gaps that passive rereading may hide.
  • Retrieval practice can strengthen long-term memory.
📌 Remember

Read less passively → Retrieve more actively

28. Retrieval Practice
  • Retrieval practice involves repeatedly attempting to recall previously learned information.
  • Retrieval itself strengthens memory.
  • Practice tests can serve as learning tools, not only assessment tools.
  • Feedback after retrieval helps correct errors.
  • Retrieval practice is more effective when the learner attempts an answer before viewing the solution.
  • Mixing retrieval with conceptual explanation improves both memory and understanding.
29. Spaced Learning
  • Spaced learning distributes study sessions over time.
  • Spaced practice is generally more effective for long-term retention than the same amount of study concentrated into one session.
  • The spacing effect refers to improved retention when learning is distributed across time.
  • Regular revision reduces forgetting.
  • Spacing is especially useful for large quantities of factual information.
  • Repeated retrieval across spaced intervals combines two powerful learning principles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spacing → Study over intervals

Cramming → Study concentrated in one period

30. Massed Practice
  • Massed practice involves concentrating learning into a short continuous period.
  • Cramming is a common form of massed practice.
  • Massed practice can create a feeling of familiarity.
  • Familiarity immediately after study does not guarantee long-term retention.
  • Spaced practice generally produces better long-term retention than massed practice.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cramming may improve immediate familiarity but often produces weaker long-term retention.

31. Forgetting
  • Forgetting is the inability to retrieve previously learned information.
  • Information may be forgotten because it was poorly encoded.
  • Lack of retrieval cues can contribute to forgetting.
  • Interference from other learning can affect recall.
  • Long periods without retrieval can weaken access to information.
  • Regular revision helps reduce forgetting.
32. Forgetting Curve
  • Hermann Ebbinghaus conducted influential experimental studies of memory and forgetting.
  • Ebbinghaus is associated with the forgetting curve.
  • The forgetting curve describes rapid loss of newly learned information followed by a slower rate of forgetting.
  • Review and retrieval help slow forgetting.
  • Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables in his memory experiments to reduce the influence of prior knowledge.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hermann Ebbinghaus → Forgetting Curve

33. Primacy and Recency Effects
  • The primacy effect refers to better memory for items presented at the beginning of a sequence.
  • The recency effect refers to better memory for items presented near the end.
  • Primacy and recency together contribute to the serial-position effect.
  • Middle items in a long unstructured list may be remembered less well than beginning and ending items.
  • Organising and revising material can reduce dependence on serial position.
📌 Remember

Primacy → Beginning

Recency → End

34. Interference
  • Interference occurs when one set of information disrupts memory for another.
  • Proactive interference occurs when old learning interferes with new learning.
  • Retroactive interference occurs when new learning interferes with previously learned information.
  • Similar information is especially susceptible to interference.
  • Clear differentiation between related concepts can reduce interference.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Proactive → Old affects New

Retroactive → New affects Old

35. Attention
  • Attention is the selective focusing of mental resources on particular information.
  • Information that receives little attention is less likely to be encoded effectively.
  • Distraction can reduce learning efficiency.
  • Divided attention can impair performance on demanding tasks.
  • Focused attention helps working memory process information.
  • Excessive simultaneous stimuli can increase cognitive load.
36. Cognitive Load
  • Cognitive load refers to the mental demand placed on working memory.
  • Working memory has limited capacity.
  • Excessive information at one time can hinder learning.
  • Breaking complex material into manageable steps reduces unnecessary cognitive load.
  • Prior knowledge reduces cognitive load by allowing information to be grouped into meaningful structures.
  • Clear diagrams can sometimes reduce the effort needed to understand complex relationships.
  • Unnecessary decorative information can distract from essential content.
37. Schema
  • A schema is an organised mental framework for representing knowledge.
  • Schemas help interpret new information.
  • Existing schemas influence how new knowledge is understood.
  • Conceptual learning develops interconnected schemas.
  • Experts generally possess richer and better-organised schemas than beginners.
  • Incorrect schemas can contribute to persistent misconceptions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Schema → Organised knowledge structure

38. Elaboration
  • Elaboration involves adding meaning and connections to new information.
  • Asking why and how questions promotes elaboration.
  • Explaining a concept in one's own words is a form of elaboration.
  • Connecting a new fact with a familiar example supports elaborative learning.
  • Elaborative learning generally produces stronger memory than mechanical repetition alone.
39. Self-Explanation
  • Self-explanation means explaining to oneself how or why something works.
  • Self-explanation can reveal gaps in understanding.
  • It encourages integration of new information with prior knowledge.
  • Explaining each step of a problem promotes conceptual learning.
  • Merely copying a worked solution does not provide the same benefit as understanding why each step is valid.
40. Learning by Examples
  • Worked examples demonstrate how a principle is applied.
  • Examples make abstract concepts easier to understand.
  • Multiple examples help learners identify the common underlying principle.
  • Using only one example can cause a learner to associate the concept too narrowly with that example.
  • Contrasting examples can highlight important differences between concepts.
41. Learning Through Experiment
  • Practical experiments connect abstract scientific concepts with observable evidence.
  • Experiments help learners test predictions.
  • Experimentation can expose misconceptions.
  • Hands-on activity is most educational when connected with explanation and reflection.
  • Performing an experiment without understanding its purpose may become another form of mechanical learning.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Experiment → Observe → Explain → Understand

42. Inquiry-Based Learning
  • Inquiry-based learning begins with questions, problems or observations.
  • Learners investigate evidence rather than receiving every conclusion directly.
  • Inquiry promotes questioning and scientific reasoning.
  • Formulating hypotheses is part of inquiry-based science learning.
  • Experimentation and data analysis support inquiry.
  • Teacher guidance may still be important in effective inquiry learning.
43. Discovery Learning
  • Discovery learning involves learners identifying principles through exploration and problem-solving.
  • Jerome Bruner is strongly associated with discovery learning.
  • Bruner emphasised active involvement in learning.
  • Discovery learning can promote conceptual understanding when learners receive appropriate guidance.
  • Pure unguided discovery may be difficult for beginners when the subject is complex.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jerome Bruner → Discovery Learning

44. Constructivism
  • Constructivism views learners as actively constructing understanding rather than merely receiving information.
  • New knowledge is interpreted through existing knowledge and experience.
  • Jean Piaget is strongly associated with cognitive constructivism.
  • Lev Vygotsky emphasised the social and cultural dimensions of learning.
  • Constructivist teaching commonly uses active problem-solving, discussion and exploration.
  • Prior misconceptions can influence how new knowledge is constructed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

Piaget → Cognitive development / Constructivism

Vygotsky → Social interaction in learning

45. Piaget and Learning
  • Jean Piaget studied cognitive development in children.
  • Piaget proposed that children actively construct knowledge through interaction with their environment.
  • Assimilation involves incorporating new information into an existing schema.
  • Accommodation involves modifying an existing schema to fit new information.
  • Adaptation involves the interaction of assimilation and accommodation.
  • Piaget proposed stages of cognitive development.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Assimilation → Fit new information into existing schema

Accommodation → Change schema

46. Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
  • Piaget proposed four major stages of cognitive development.
  • Sensorimotor stage approximately covers birth to 2 years.
  • Preoperational stage approximately covers 2 to 7 years.
  • Concrete operational stage approximately covers 7 to 11 years.
  • Formal operational stage begins approximately around 11 years and continues into adulthood.
  • Abstract and hypothetical reasoning develops strongly during the formal operational stage.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Sensorimotor → Preoperational → Concrete Operational → Formal Operational

47. Vygotsky and Learning
  • Lev Vygotsky emphasised the importance of social interaction in cognitive development.
  • Vygotsky proposed the concept of the Zone of Proximal Development.
  • The Zone of Proximal Development refers to tasks a learner cannot yet perform independently but can perform with appropriate assistance.
  • Learning can be supported through guidance from teachers or more capable peers.
  • Scaffolding refers to temporary support given to help a learner perform a task.
  • Support is gradually reduced as competence develops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vygotsky → ZPD → Scaffolding → Social Learning

48. Scaffolding
  • Scaffolding is temporary instructional support given to a learner.
  • Scaffolding may include hints, prompts, demonstrations or partially completed solutions.
  • Effective scaffolding is gradually withdrawn as the learner becomes more independent.
  • Scaffolding helps learners perform tasks that are initially beyond their unaided ability.
  • The term is closely associated with teaching based on Vygotskian ideas.
49. Bloom's Taxonomy
  • Bloom's taxonomy is a framework for classifying educational learning objectives.
  • Benjamin Bloom was associated with the original taxonomy published in 1956.
  • The original cognitive levels included knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation.
  • A revised taxonomy was published by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl and colleagues in 2001.
  • The revised taxonomy uses the levels Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create.
  • The revised taxonomy places Create above Evaluate.
📌 Must-Memorise Revised Sequence

Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create

50. Bloom's Taxonomy and Learning
  • Remembering mainly involves retrieving facts.
  • Understanding involves explaining meaning.
  • Applying involves using knowledge in a situation.
  • Analysing involves breaking information into parts and examining relationships.
  • Evaluating involves making judgements using criteria.
  • Creating involves producing a new product, plan or solution.
  • Rote learning operates mainly at the remembering level.
  • Conceptual learning supports understanding, application and higher-order thinking.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rote → Remember

Conceptual → Understand + Apply + Higher-order thinking

51. Lower-Order and Higher-Order Thinking
  • Remembering and basic understanding are commonly treated as lower-order cognitive processes.
  • Application, analysis, evaluation and creation require progressively more complex thinking.
  • Higher-order thinking requires more than simple recall.
  • Problem-solving often involves application and analysis.
  • Scientific reasoning frequently requires analysis, evaluation and creation of explanations.
52. Metacognition
  • Metacognition means thinking about one's own thinking and learning.
  • Metacognition includes knowing what one understands and what remains unclear.
  • Planning study is a metacognitive activity.
  • Monitoring one's comprehension is a metacognitive activity.
  • Evaluating the effectiveness of a study method is a metacognitive activity.
  • Self-testing improves metacognitive accuracy by revealing actual recall.
  • Learners can feel familiar with a topic without being able to retrieve or apply it.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Metacognition → Plan → Monitor → Evaluate

53. Feedback
  • Feedback provides information about performance or understanding.
  • Effective feedback identifies errors and guides improvement.
  • Immediate feedback can help correct misconceptions before they become established.
  • Feedback is more useful when it explains why an answer is incorrect rather than merely stating that it is wrong.
  • Learners should use feedback to modify future strategies.
  • Feedback combined with active practice promotes learning.
54. Practice
  • Practice strengthens skills and improves retrieval.
  • Repetition alone can improve speed and familiarity.
  • Deliberate practice focuses on specific weaknesses and includes feedback.
  • Practice should include varied examples to improve transfer.
  • Solving the same type of problem repeatedly may produce procedural familiarity without deeper understanding.
  • Mixed practice can require learners to identify which principle should be used.
55. Interleaving
  • Interleaving involves mixing different types of problems or topics during practice.
  • Interleaving differs from practising one type of problem repeatedly in a single block.
  • Interleaving can improve the ability to distinguish between problem types.
  • It encourages selection of the appropriate method rather than mechanically repeating the same procedure.
  • Interleaving may feel more difficult during practice but can improve later discrimination and application.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blocked Practice → Same type together

Interleaving → Different types mixed

56. Concept Mapping
  • A concept map visually represents relationships among concepts.
  • Concepts are connected using labelled links.
  • Concept maps help organise knowledge hierarchically or relationally.
  • They can reveal misconceptions and missing connections.
  • Joseph D. Novak is strongly associated with the development of concept mapping.
  • Concept maps were influenced by Ausubel's theory of meaningful learning.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joseph Novak → Concept Maps

Ausubel → Meaningful Learning

57. Mind Map vs Concept Map
  • A mind map commonly radiates ideas from a central topic.
  • A concept map explicitly shows relationships among concepts using connecting links.
  • Both can help organise information.
  • Concept maps are particularly useful for showing conceptual relationships.
  • Neither method alone guarantees understanding.
58. Problem-Based Learning
  • Problem-based learning begins with a meaningful problem.
  • Learners identify what they need to know in order to solve the problem.
  • It encourages application of knowledge.
  • It develops reasoning and collaborative problem-solving.
  • Problems should be sufficiently structured or guided for the learner's level.
59. Collaborative Learning
  • Collaborative learning involves learners working together toward a learning goal.
  • Explaining concepts to others can improve understanding.
  • Discussion exposes learners to alternative reasoning.
  • Group work is effective when participants actively engage rather than merely divide work mechanically.
  • Peer explanation can reveal misconceptions.
60. Learning by Teaching
  • Explaining a topic to another person requires retrieval and organisation of knowledge.
  • Teaching a concept can expose gaps in one's understanding.
  • Effective explanation requires understanding relationships rather than merely reciting words.
  • Preparing to teach can increase attention to structure and meaning.
61. Rote Learning — Appropriate Uses
  • Exact scientific definitions may require memorisation.
  • Chemical symbols require memorisation.
  • SI units require memorisation.
  • Scientific constants may require memorisation.
  • Biological names often require memorisation.
  • Anatomical terminology may require memorisation.
  • Formulae may need to be remembered before they can be applied.
  • Sequences such as taxonomic ranks may require memorisation.
  • Factual recall provides essential building blocks for higher-level reasoning.
📌 Remember

Memorise facts that must be known exactly.

Understand relationships that must be applied.

62. Limitations of Pure Rote Learning
  • Pure rote learning may produce shallow understanding.
  • Memorised procedures may fail when a problem is presented differently.
  • Rote knowledge can be difficult to transfer to unfamiliar situations.
  • Mechanical memorisation may encourage confusion between similar concepts.
  • Knowledge learned without meaningful connections may be forgotten more rapidly.
  • Correct recall does not automatically imply scientific understanding.
63. Advantages of Conceptual Learning
  • Conceptual learning supports long-term understanding.
  • It improves transfer to new situations.
  • It strengthens problem-solving.
  • It helps learners reconstruct forgotten details from underlying principles.
  • It enables comparison between related ideas.
  • It facilitates integration of information from different topics.
  • It makes it easier to identify errors and misconceptions.
64. Limitations of Conceptual Learning Without Factual Knowledge
  • Conceptual reasoning requires a foundation of relevant facts.
  • A learner cannot efficiently reason about scientific concepts without knowing essential terminology.
  • Important formulas must often be recalled before they can be applied.
  • Lack of factual knowledge increases working-memory demands.
  • Experts reason effectively partly because they possess extensive organised factual knowledge.
  • Conceptual understanding and factual recall should therefore complement each other.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Facts versus concepts is not an either-or choice.

Strong learning requires both.

65. Scientific Learning
  • Science learning requires both factual knowledge and conceptual understanding.
  • Knowing that force is measured in newtons is factual knowledge.
  • Understanding how force changes motion is conceptual knowledge.
  • Knowing Ohm's law as V = IR is factual recall.
  • Using V = IR correctly in a new circuit problem requires conceptual and procedural understanding.
  • Memorising a biological process is weaker than understanding the relationships among its stages.
  • Experiments help link theory with observable evidence.
66. Procedural Knowledge
  • Procedural knowledge is knowledge of how to perform a task.
  • Solving an equation uses procedural knowledge.
  • Operating laboratory equipment involves procedural knowledge.
  • Procedural fluency improves with practice.
  • Procedures are most transferable when learners also understand why each step works.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Declarative → Know what

Procedural → Know how

Conceptual → Know why / relationships

67. Declarative Knowledge
  • Declarative knowledge refers to factual information that can be stated.
  • Scientific definitions are examples of declarative knowledge.
  • Names, dates, symbols and units are declarative knowledge.
  • Declarative knowledge is important but does not by itself guarantee application skill.
  • Retrieval practice is useful for strengthening declarative knowledge.
68. Conceptual Knowledge
  • Conceptual knowledge involves understanding relationships among facts and ideas.
  • It includes categories, principles, models and generalisations.
  • Conceptual knowledge allows facts to be organised meaningfully.
  • Scientific laws and principles form part of conceptual knowledge.
  • Strong conceptual knowledge supports inference and problem-solving.
69. Learning Outcomes
  • A learning outcome describes what a learner should be able to know or do after learning.
  • Recall-based outcomes ask learners to remember information.
  • Understanding-based outcomes ask learners to explain ideas.
  • Application outcomes require using knowledge in a situation.
  • Analytical outcomes require identifying relationships or components.
  • Clear learning outcomes guide appropriate teaching and assessment.
70. Assessment of Rote and Conceptual Learning
  • Direct factual questions primarily test recall.
  • Explanation questions test understanding.
  • Application questions test transfer of knowledge.
  • Novel problem-solving questions can reveal conceptual understanding.
  • Asking learners to justify an answer reveals reasoning.
  • Multiple-choice questions can test either recall or conceptual understanding depending on how they are designed.
  • Memorising previous answers may produce high scores without deep understanding if assessment contains only repeated questions.
71. Common TNPSC Learning Pairs
  • Rote learning → Repetition and recall.
  • Conceptual learning → Understanding and application.
  • Recall → Retrieve information.
  • Recognition → Identify familiar information.

  • Chunking → Grouping information.

  • Negative transfer → Previous learning interferes.

  • Metacognition → Thinking about one's own learning.
72. Important Personalities
  • Hermann Ebbinghaus → Experimental study of memory and forgetting.
  • David Ausubel → Meaningful learning and importance of prior knowledge.
  • Jean Piaget → Cognitive development and constructivist learning.
  • Lev Vygotsky → Social learning and Zone of Proximal Development.
  • Jerome Bruner → Discovery learning.
  • Benjamin Bloom → Taxonomy of educational objectives.
  • Joseph Novak → Concept mapping.
  • Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl → Revised Bloom's taxonomy.
73. TNPSC Traps
  • Rote learning and conceptual learning are not complete opposites that can never coexist.
  • Memorisation does not automatically produce understanding.
  • Understanding does not eliminate the need to remember facts.
  • Recognition is generally easier than recall.
  • Rereading is not the same as active retrieval.
  • Cramming and spaced learning are not identical.
  • Short-term familiarity after cramming does not guarantee long-term retention.
  • Proactive interference means old learning affects new learning.
  • Retroactive interference means new learning affects old learning.
  • Positive transfer helps learning; negative transfer interferes.
  • A misconception is not simply a forgotten fact.
  • Working memory has limited capacity.
  • Chunking does not increase knowledge by itself; it organises information more efficiently.
  • A mnemonic aids memory but does not explain a concept.
  • Bloom's revised taxonomy uses Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create.
  • Create is the highest level in the revised Bloom taxonomy.
  • Ausubel is associated with meaningful learning.
  • Bruner is associated with discovery learning.
  • Vygotsky is associated with the Zone of Proximal Development.
  • Novak is associated with concept maps.
  • Ebbinghaus is associated with the forgetting curve.

  • Learning mainly through repetition? → Rote learning.
  • Learning through understanding relationships? → Conceptual learning.
  • Best suited for exact factual recall? → Rote learning.
  • Best suited for applying knowledge to new situations? → Conceptual learning.
  • Can rote learning be useful? → Yes, for essential facts, definitions, symbols, units and formulas.
  • Does conceptual learning remove the need for factual knowledge? → No.
  • Retrieving information without seeing the answer? → Recall.
  • Identifying previously encountered information? → Recognition.
  • Which is usually easier: recall or recognition? → Recognition.
  • Three basic memory processes? → Encoding, storage and retrieval.
  • Visual sensory memory? → Iconic memory.
  • Auditory sensory memory? → Echoic memory.
  • Temporary active processing system? → Working memory.
  • Memory system with limited capacity? → Working memory.
  • Extended storage of information? → Long-term memory.
  • Simple repetition? → Maintenance rehearsal.
  • Connecting information with meaning? → Elaborative rehearsal.
  • Theory of meaningful learning associated with? → David Ausubel.
  • New knowledge should be linked with? → Prior knowledge.
  • Incorrect understanding of a concept? → Misconception.
  • Grouping information into meaningful units? → Chunking.
  • Memory aid? → Mnemonic.
  • Application of previous learning to a new situation? → Transfer of learning.
  • Previous learning helps new learning? → Positive transfer.
  • Previous learning interferes with new learning? → Negative transfer.
  • Old information interferes with new information? → Proactive interference.
  • New information interferes with old information? → Retroactive interference.
  • Deliberately retrieving information from memory? → Active recall.
  • Repeated self-testing is called? → Retrieval practice.
  • Study distributed over time? → Spaced practice.
  • Concentrated study in one period? → Massed practice or cramming.
  • Effect showing benefit of distributed revision? → Spacing effect.
  • Forgetting curve associated with? → Hermann Ebbinghaus.
  • Better memory for beginning items? → Primacy effect.
  • Better memory for ending items? → Recency effect.
  • Primacy + recency together form? → Serial-position effect.
  • Selective focusing of mental resources? → Attention.
  • Mental demand placed on working memory? → Cognitive load.
  • Organised mental framework of knowledge? → Schema.
  • Adding meaningful connections to information? → Elaboration.
  • Explaining a concept to oneself? → Self-explanation.
  • Learning by investigating questions and evidence? → Inquiry-based learning.
  • Discovery learning associated with? → Jerome Bruner.
  • Cognitive constructivism associated with? → Jean Piaget.
  • Social approach to learning associated with? → Lev Vygotsky.
  • Zone of Proximal Development associated with? → Vygotsky.
  • Temporary instructional support? → Scaffolding.
  • Piaget's first stage? → Sensorimotor.
  • Piaget's second stage? → Preoperational.
  • Piaget's third stage? → Concrete operational.
  • Piaget's fourth stage? → Formal operational.
  • Assimilation means? → Fitting new information into an existing schema.
  • Accommodation means? → Modifying a schema to fit new information.
  • Bloom's taxonomy associated with? → Benjamin Bloom.
  • Original Bloom taxonomy published? → 1956.
  • Revised Bloom taxonomy published? → 2001.
  • First level of revised Bloom taxonomy? → Remember.
  • Highest level of revised Bloom taxonomy? → Create.
  • Revised Bloom sequence? → Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create.
  • Thinking about one's own thinking? → Metacognition.
  • Three basic metacognitive processes? → Plan, monitor and evaluate.
  • Mixing different problem types during practice? → Interleaving.
  • Practising one type repeatedly before another? → Blocked practice.
  • Concept maps strongly associated with? → Joseph Novak.
  • Concept mapping was influenced by whose meaningful learning theory? → David Ausubel.
  • Knowledge of facts? → Declarative knowledge.
  • Knowledge of how to perform a task? → Procedural knowledge.
  • Knowledge of relationships and principles? → Conceptual knowledge.
  • Is memorising V = IR alone conceptual understanding? → No.
  • Applying V = IR correctly to a new situation demonstrates? → Application and conceptual/procedural understanding.
  • Best overall learning approach for science? → Combine accurate factual recall with conceptual understanding and application.
